clue.text: Approbation from a lying Irishman?

parts.note: a gesture of praise, read as an Irishman called Pat lying flat on his spine

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether praise from a fibbing Irishman is worth anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lying' suggests telling untruths, but it means lying down: Pat, the stock Irish name, stretched out supine.
explanation.definitionFit: A congratulatory slap between the shoulders is a familiar token of approval, and the phrase means praise generally.

clue.text: Leave the bank — is there going to be a row?

definitions.text: is there going to be a row?

explanation.surface: Someone about to cast off from the riverbank wonders whether a quarrel is brewing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' looks like a quarrel; it is rowing a boat, which begins once you shove away from the shore.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoving a boat away from the shore is how you depart the bank, and it is the start of an outing with oars.

clue.text: Print a quarter of Melville's work

parts.note: to print is to set in type
east, one of the four compass quarters, abbreviated E

explanation.surface: A printer is asked to run off part of a Melville book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A quarter of' looks like a fraction of the novel; it is a compass point, E for east.
explanation.definitionFit: Herman Melville's first book, an 1846 South Seas adventure, carries this title.

clue.text: Word coined in Giles' moon trip

indicators.note: a trip is a stumble, so these letters fall over into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone named Giles invents a new term while travelling to the moon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trip' looks like a journey; it is the anagram signal on GILES MOON.
explanation.definitionFit: A newly invented term or expression is a coinage of language.

clue.text: Subject of old German hymn

parts.note: the 1914 German 'Hymn of' this, a song of loathing aimed at England

explanation.surface: A question about the theme of a historic German church song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hymn' suggests worship, but Ernst Lissauer's 1914 poem 'Hassgesang gegen England' is the 'Hymn of Hate', a wartime song of loathing.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous 1914 'Hymn of Hate' took loathing of England as its theme.

clue.text: Refreshment place opening in old Merionethshire

definitions.note: the definition stands for a town situated in that former Welsh county

parts.note: a bar is a place serving drinks
a mouth is an opening, as of a river or cave

explanation.surface: A café sits at the entrance of something in a former Welsh county.
explanation.walkthrough: Merionethshire was a Welsh county abolished in 1974; the definition means 'a place in' it, a seaside town at the mouth of the Mawddach estuary.
explanation.definitionFit: The resort town stands on the Cardigan Bay coast of what was Merionethshire before Welsh county reorganisation.

clue.text: A lot of people exult over dunderhead

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece written over another comes first

parts.note: to crow is to boast or exult
the head of 'dunder', its first letter, is D

explanation.surface: A throng gloats at a fool's expense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dunderhead' looks like an insult; split, it is the head of 'dunder', the letter D.
explanation.definitionFit: A throng or mass of people is a crowd.

clue.text: Miss foreign notaries' embarrassment

indicators.note: embarrassment throws the letters into confusion, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A young lady abroad is mortified by some lawyers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss' looks like a verb; with 'foreign' it is a young unmarried woman abroad, in Spanish usage. 'Embarrassment' rearranges NOTARIES.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish title for an unmarried young woman is the equivalent of the English courtesy title.

clue.text: Report includes the same savage animal

indicators.note: includes means one piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: a report is a loud bang
do is short for ditto, meaning the same

explanation.surface: A news report covers the same wild beast again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' looks like a news story; it is a loud noise. DO, short for ditto, goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A chained mastiff-type guard dog, known for ferocity, was given this old name.

clue.text: Someone encouraging us, perhaps to eat and drink

parts.note: to sup is to take supper, to eat
porter is a dark beer

explanation.surface: A friend urges us to have food and a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs to 'perhaps': a fan cheering us on is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A fan or backer who cheers someone on is one who gives them support.

clue.text: Ending love by returning a jewel

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O

indicators.note: returning means the words for a jewel are read backwards

parts.note: a gem is a jewel

explanation.surface: A romance ends when a ring is given back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returning' turns A GEM into MEGA, which follows O.
explanation.definitionFit: The last letter of the Greek alphabet stands for the end of anything.

clue.text: Catty creature has nothing to do with the church set

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O
CE stands for Church of England
a lot is a set or batch

explanation.surface: A spiteful person refuses to mix with the parish crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catty' suggests spitefulness; it means cat-like, a spotted wild cat.
explanation.definitionFit: This spotted American wild cat is a feline, so cat-like.

clue.text: Praise for the bowler, of course!

explanation.surface: A bowls club cheers a player, as expected.
explanation.walkthrough: In lawn bowls 'good wood' is a cry of approval for a fine delivery; 'of course' points to the Sussex racecourse of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Bowlers applaud a well-placed wood with this phrase, and the same name belongs to a famous Sussex horse-racing venue.

clue.text: Wood has ink mixed in cask

parts.note: fir is a type of wood

indicators.note: mixed means the letters are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: Some timber gets ink spilt in a barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixed' rearranges INK into KIN after FIR.
explanation.definitionFit: A small barrel holding a quarter of a beer barrel goes by this old measure name.

clue.text: Merrymaker has about £2, always wants a rise

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the whole string is written bottom to top

parts.note: re means about or concerning
the pound sign stands for L (libra), so two pounds is L twice
ever means always

explanation.surface: A party-goer who already has a couple of pounds keeps wanting a pay increase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wants a rise' sounds like a pay claim; it turns RE + LL + EVER (RELLEVER) upwards in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A party-goer who revels is one making merry.

clue.text: Accommodation suited to house hunters, perhaps

definitions.text: Accommodation suited to house hunters, perhaps

parts.words: Accommodation suited to house hunters, perhaps
parts.note: lodging for horses ridden to hounds, called hunters

explanation.surface: Somewhere to live for people looking to buy a home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House hunters' looks like property buyers; 'house' is a verb and hunters are horses used for fox-hunting.
explanation.definitionFit: Lodging for horses in stalls is provided by this kind of accommodation.

clue.text: Flower holds the means of improving parsnips?

definitions.text: Flower holds the means of improving parsnips?

parts.words: Flower holds the means of improving parsnips?
parts.note: a yellow wild flower read as a vessel for the spread said to dress up root vegetables

explanation.surface: A gardener wonders whether some bloom contains the secret to better root vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'fine words butter no parsnips' implies butter is what improves parsnips; this flower's name reads as a cup holding it.
explanation.definitionFit: A yellow meadow flower of the ranunculus family has a name that literally means a cup for dairy spread.

clue.text: Walker's sound-didn't get drunk

explanation.surface: A rambler's footsteps go unnoticed because they stayed sober.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the dregs left in the bottom of glasses, the drink not swallowed.
explanation.definitionFit: The noise of a pedestrian's shoes striking the pavement, and the leftover liquor at the bottom of glasses after drinking.

clue.text: One of twelve of the fiery fifth

definitions.text: One of twelve of the fiery fifth

parts.words: One of twelve of the fiery fifth
parts.note: a month of the year, the one whose fifth day is bonfire night

explanation.surface: Something belongs to a dozen connected with a blazing date.
explanation.walkthrough: The fiery fifth is Guy Fawkes Night, a British celebration with bonfires and fireworks on the fifth of this month.
explanation.definitionFit: The calendar has twelve months, and Bonfire Night falls on the fifth of this autumn one.

clue.text: This one is oneself

parts.note: add 'one' to the answer and the phrase means looking after yourself first

explanation.surface: A statement about personal identity.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'number one' is slang for oneself, as in 'look after number one'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'number one' means oneself, so this word followed by 'one' gives self.

clue.text: Animals go to the porch the back way

parts.note: a stoa is a classical Greek porch or colonnade

indicators.note: back means the word for way is turned round

parts.note: St is short for street, a way

explanation.surface: Some creatures wander round to the rear entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The back way' looks like a route; 'back' turns ST (street) into TS after STOA.
explanation.definitionFit: Small brown carnivores related to weasels are wild animals.

clue.text: He might make a bad inside right

definitions.text: He might make a bad inside right

parts.words: He might make a bad inside right
parts.note: a doctor who corrects internal disorders, disguised as a football position

explanation.surface: A football coach judges a player unsuited to the inside-right position.
explanation.walkthrough: Inside right is an old football position; read again, it means making diseased innards healthy.
explanation.definitionFit: An operating doctor repairs damaged internal organs.

clue.text: Breakwater clue Is wrong? Small matter

parts.note: a mole is a stone pier or breakwater

indicators.note: wrong means the letters are put in the wrong order, rearranged

explanation.surface: A solver wonders whether a clue about a harbour wall is wrong, but it matters little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small matter' sounds dismissive; it is a tiny particle of matter. 'Wrong' rearranges CLUE into CULE.
explanation.definitionFit: The smallest unit of a chemical compound is a tiny particle of matter.

clue.text: Sleuths about to knock back drink

parts.note: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, British police detectives

indicators.note: to knock back reverses the word for about

parts.note: re means about

explanation.surface: Detectives are about to down a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To knock back' looks like drinking; it turns RE into ER after CID.
explanation.definitionFit: This fermented apple juice is an alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Go about two

parts.note: re means about or concerning
a pair is two

explanation.surface: A terse instruction to travel round as a couple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go' is the definition in its sense 'betake oneself', as in 'repair to the bar'.
explanation.definitionFit: To betake oneself somewhere, as in withdrawing to the drawing room, has this formal verb.

clue.text: Tropical bird has a leg on one

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece written on another sits above it

parts.note: gam is slang for a leg
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: An exotic bird stands on one leg.
explanation.walkthrough: GAM is old slang for a leg; the bird is the trumpeter of South America.
explanation.definitionFit: The trumpeter of South American rainforests is known by this name.

clue.text: An employer's crafty ruse

indicators.note: something crafty is artfully twisted, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A boss is guilty of a cunning trick.
explanation.walkthrough: An employer is one who employs or uses something; 'crafty' rearranges RUSE. The grid's first letter is unchecked.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who employs a thing makes use of it.

clue.text: Some trouble men don't correct

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some difficulties go unfixed by the men responsible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes part of 'troublE MEN Don't'.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to remove its errors.

clue.text: Companion shows nothing in case it's a mistake

indicators.note: in means the zero goes inside the rearranged letters
a mistake means the letters have been put in the wrong order

parts.note: taken as its letters, the apostrophe ignored
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A partner proves blameless in case there is an error.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A mistake' rearranges CASE ITS A, and 'in' places O inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A partner or colleague one keeps company with is a companion.

clue.text: It may reduce ill-feeling, before writing in about nothing

parts.note: pre means before
script is handwriting

indicators.note: about means the word in goes round the zero

parts.note: taken as written
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: Something to ease bad feeling comes before writing about nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ill-feeling' looks like resentment; it means sickness, eased by a doctor's written order for medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor's written order for medicine aims to cure sickness.
